platforms.title: Eyelid Twitching: It's Probably Not Magnesium — It's This
platforms.meta_description: Magnesium gets blamed first, but NIH-indexed research found no link to eyelid twitching. Caffeine and fatigue have much stronger evidence.
platforms.body_html:
The moment an eyelid starts twitching, most people reach for a magnesium supplement. It's the most-searched fix — but according to a clinical review on eyelid myokymia indexed on the NIH's StatPearls database, two separate cross-sectional studies found no association between blood magnesium levels and benign eyelid twitching. The mineral everyone blames first isn't actually the best-supported cause.

Caffeine and Fatigue — Not Magnesium — Have the Real Evidence

That same review notes that fatigue is a contributing factor in roughly 60 percent of chronic myokymia cases, and that caffeine increases the sensitivity of the nerve signals feeding the small muscles around the eye, making them more prone to firing on their own. Mayo Clinic lists stress, tiredness, and caffeine as the most common everyday triggers of eye twitching. None of this means magnesium plays zero role for anyone — some people do notice improvement — but the evidence for it is far thinner than the evidence for cutting back on coffee and catching up on sleep.

Screen time adds another layer. Eye strain from hours of close-up screen work and the dry eye that comes with reduced blinking have both been linked to eyelid twitching in the same clinical literature, which is why the twitch often shows up at the end of a long workday rather than first thing in the morning.

Two More Triggers That Get Less Attention

Caffeine and fatigue dominate the conversation, but clinical descriptions of eyelid twitching also mention dehydration and alcohol almost as often — they just get less attention because they're less talked about online. Alcohol has a mild diuretic effect and can disrupt the depth of sleep even when it doesn't fully wake you up, which stacks on top of whatever fatigue is already contributing to the twitch. Dehydration on its own can also make nerve and muscle signaling slightly less stable, and it's an easy thing to overlook on a day that's already busy enough to cause stress in the first place.

Because several of these triggers tend to cluster together — a late night out, less sleep, more coffee the next morning to compensate, maybe a drink or two — it's often hard to isolate just one culprit from memory alone. A simple two-week log of caffeine intake, sleep hours, and alcohol, jotted down whenever the twitch shows up, tends to reveal the pattern faster than guessing. Most people find one or two triggers repeat far more than the others once they actually look at it written down.

What to Actually Change First

  • Cut caffeine for one to two weeks before anything else. If the twitch fades or shows up less often, caffeine was likely driving it.
  • Protect sleep before reaching for a supplement. With fatigue behind the majority of chronic cases, more consistent sleep often does more than any pill.
  • Take real screen breaks. Looking away every 20 minutes reduces the eye strain and dry eye that can trigger the same twitch.

When It's Worth Seeing a Doctor

Benign eyelid myokymia is almost always harmless and fades on its own within days to a couple of weeks. It's worth getting checked by an eye doctor or neurologist if the twitching lasts more than a few weeks, if the eyelid closes completely during a spasm, or if the twitching spreads to other muscles in the face — those patterns point to a different, less common condition than ordinary myokymia, and they're not something to self-diagnose from an article. This content is general health information, not a diagnosis.
